did_you_know.text: The title identifies Psalm 52 as a “maskil of David”—a psalm with an instructive and guiding character, encouraging readers to reflect on the consequences of wickedness and the value of faithfulness to God.

The psalm mentions Doeg the Edomite and his report to Saul about David’s arrival at the house of Ahimelech, thereby connecting the psalm’s words with the act of informing that harmed Ahimelech’s household.
The psalmist condemns boasting in evil and contrasts it with God’s steadfast love, described as enduring “all day long.”
The wicked person’s tongue is described as “a sharpened razor”—a sharp, honed blade—an image showing how deceitful words can cause harm.
The psalm presents a stark moral reversal: the wicked person loves evil more than good, falsehood more than righteousness, and every word that destroys and every deceitful tongue.
The wicked person’s punishment is described through three images of uprooting and loss: God will tear him down, cut him off, and sweep him away from his tent and from the land of the living.
The downfall of the wicked serves as a warning to the righteous: they see it, fear the seriousness of the judgment, and even mock the one who trusted in his evil ways.
The verse contrasts the person who does not make God his stronghold and trusts in his great wealth and evil deeds with those who place their trust in God.
The psalmist compares himself to a “green olive tree” in God’s house—a picture of vitality, stability, and blessing—and attributes this to his trust in God’s steadfast love.
The psalm concludes with two expressions of faith: continual thanksgiving for God’s deeds and hope in his good name in the presence of his faithful people.
